clue.text: They reflect certainly after musical ending in failure

parts.note: Cats is the Andrew Lloyd Webber musical

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter, so only the last letter of failure is used

parts.note: its last letter is E
yes, certainly: an affirmative reply

explanation.surface: Someone comments on a musical that ended in failure, and the cast reflect on it ruefully.
explanation.walkthrough: Cat's eyes are the glass studs set into British roads that bounce back car headlights; 'reflect' looks like 'ponder' in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Cat's eyes are road studs whose job is to bounce car headlights back to the driver at night.

clue.text: Happen to see end of play, memorable

parts.note: to catch a show is to happen to see it

indicators.note: end of means only the final letter of play is used

parts.note: its last letter is Y

explanation.surface: Someone happens to see the end of a play and finds it memorable.
explanation.definitionFit: A catchy tune is one that is easy to remember and sticks in the mind.

clue.text: Leader in trade to study factory's boring routine

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, so only the start of trade is taken

parts.note: its first letter is T
to read a subject is to study it at university
a mill is a factory; the 's is read as 'is', a link

explanation.surface: A factory worker leading in trade studies the dull routine of the shop floor.
explanation.definitionFit: A treadmill, literally an exercise machine, is figuratively a tedious unchanging cycle of work.

clue.text: Record poem about isles for part of series

indicators.note: about means around, so the record and poem go round the isles letters

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record
an ode is a lyric poem
Is. is the map abbreviation for isles

explanation.surface: A record of a poem about islands forms part of a series.
explanation.definitionFit: An episode is a single instalment of a television or radio serial.

clue.text: Brilliance of chapter in climbing story

indicators.note: the chapter letter is placed within the story word
in a down clue climbing means reading upwards, so the story word is reversed

parts.note: a tale is a story

explanation.surface: The brilliance of a chapter in an adventure story about climbing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climbing' turns TALE upwards to ELAT, and 'in' puts C inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Eclat is a French borrowing meaning dazzling success or conspicuous brilliance of effect.

clue.text: Aircon in a double-decker? You can count on it

indicators.note: the aircon letters are placed in the middle of the vehicle phrase

parts.note: a double-decker is a bus with two floors
AC is the usual abbreviation for air conditioning

explanation.surface: A question about whether a double-decker bus has air conditioning, answered with a reassurance.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a pun: an abacus is a frame of beads you literally count on.
explanation.definitionFit: An abacus is a bead frame used for arithmetic, so it is quite literally something for counting on.

clue.text: Extremely cold, close to fen, for this marsh bird?

parts.note: bitter weather is extremely cold

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only the last letter of fen is taken

parts.note: its last letter is N

explanation.surface: A question whether this marsh bird is out in the bitter cold near the fen.
explanation.definitionFit: The bittern is a shy heron that lives in reedbeds and wetlands, famous for its booming call.

clue.text: Meet Charlie, Scottish explorer

parts.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
Sir John Ross was a Scottish Arctic explorer

explanation.surface: An instruction to meet someone called Charlie, a Scottish explorer.
explanation.definitionFit: When two lines or paths cross, they intersect, which is to meet.

clue.text: Southern playwright entertaining foremost of runners — Bolt, perhaps

indicators.note: to entertain is to host, so the other piece goes inside

parts.note: Harold Pinter was a British playwright

indicators.note: the foremost letter is the first, so only the start of runners is taken

parts.note: its first letter is R

explanation.surface: A Southern playwright entertains the leading runners, Usain Bolt among them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' marks Usain Bolt, the Jamaican Olympic champion, as one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Usain Bolt, the 100m world record holder, is the best-known example of a short-distance runner.

clue.text: See, at the bubbly, an art connoisseur?

indicators.note: bubbly means effervescent, so the letters fizz into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: An invitation to see an art connoisseur sipping champagne, bubbly being slang for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bubbly' looks like a noun for champagne; it is the anagram signal working on SEE AT THE.
explanation.definitionFit: An aesthete is a person with a refined appreciation of beauty and the arts.

clue.text: Archetypal female in detox — loner, right? Sadly

indicators.note: sadly suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters of the three words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A woman in a detox clinic, a loner, is asking whether she is right, a sad picture.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is DETOX LONER RIGHT; 'in' is a link word and the dash and question mark are punctuation.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the stereotypical wholesome, approachable young woman who lives nearby, a stock character of film and fiction.

clue.text: Mostly ghastly, and tense, retreat

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all of the word, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: hideous means ghastly, very ugly
T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: Someone, ghastly and tense, beats a retreat.
explanation.definitionFit: A hideout is a hiding place or refuge, a place one retreats to; here retreat is a noun.

clue.text: Tribunal, primarily, needs to be given motive for crime

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the first letter of tribunal is taken

parts.note: its first letter is T
a reason is a motive for doing something

explanation.surface: A tribunal must be given a motive before it can rule on a crime.
explanation.definitionFit: Treason, betraying one's country or sovereign, is among the gravest of offences in law.

clue.text: Dog in Yorkshire river with tangled lead

parts.note: the Aire is a river in Yorkshire, flowing through Leeds

indicators.note: a tangled lead is twisted up, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dog splashing in a Yorkshire river has got its lead tangled.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of LEAD gives DALE, a fitting word for Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The Airedale is a large terrier breed named after the valley of the Aire in Yorkshire.

clue.text: Stress involving one daughter in casualty

indicators.note: involving means surrounding, so the stress word goes around the rest

parts.note: an accent is stress placed on a syllable
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Stress for a family with one daughter in the casualty department.
explanation.walkthrough: Casualty is the British name for a hospital emergency department, but here it means a mishap.
explanation.definitionFit: In an older sense a casualty is a chance mishap or misfortune, which is what an accident is.

clue.text: Snare, so revolutionary, shown during one broadcast

indicators.note: during places the turned word within the scrambled other word
to broadcast is to scatter, so the letters of one are spread about
something revolutionary turns round, so so is read backwards

explanation.surface: A trap, so revolutionary, is shown during a broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snare' could be a drum in a broadcast surface, but here it is a trap; the turned pair lands after the first letter of the jumbled word.
explanation.definitionFit: A noose is a loop of rope or wire that tightens when pulled, used as a trap for animals.

clue.text: In a precarious position in hot foggy French city

indicators.note: foggy means confused, so the letters of in hot are muddled

parts.note: Nice is a city on the French Riviera

explanation.surface: Being in a precarious position in a hot, foggy French city.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal covers only the clue's second 'in' and 'hot', giving ONTHI.
explanation.definitionFit: To be on thin ice is an idiom for being in a risky situation that could collapse at any moment.

clue.text: Blow for a seasonal farmer worker?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a wild swinging punch
second meaning: someone who makes hay during the summer harvest

explanation.walkthrough: 'for a' links the two senses; the question mark flags the literal reading of a punch name.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a powerful roundhouse punch and a farm hand who cuts and dries grass in summer.

clue.text: A Democrat and Liberal wing it

explanation.surface: A Democrat and a Liberal are politicians improvising, with 'wing' hinting at the political left wing.
explanation.definitionFit: To ad-lib is to speak without preparation, to improvise, which is what winging it means.

clue.text: Comprehensive cover?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a ... ban or policy covers everything
second meaning: a bed covering made of wool or similar

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it sounds like an insurance policy; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an adjective for all-inclusive and a noun for a warm bedspread.

clue.text: Wood preservative, very big over in Greek island

indicators.note: the size and cricket letters go in the middle of the island

parts.note: Crete is the largest Greek island
OS is the clothing abbreviation for outsize
O is the cricket abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: A very big wood preservative tin is shipped over to a Greek island.
explanation.walkthrough: An over is a set of six balls in cricket, abbreviated O.
explanation.definitionFit: Creosote is the dark oily tar-based liquid painted on fences and sheds to protect timber from rot.

clue.text: Take the Spanish female supporters climbing

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means reading upwards, so the pieces are reversed

parts.note: el is Spanish for the
fans are supporters

explanation.surface: Take the Spanish women's football supporters up a mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climbing' turns ELFFANS upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To snaffle is an informal British word for to take something quickly, often without permission.

clue.text: Really popular act

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
a deed is an act

explanation.walkthrough: Read as a pair it sounds like a review of a popular stage act.
explanation.definitionFit: Indeed is an adverb of emphasis meaning truly, used to confirm what was said.

clue.text: Relish slander involving big name

indicators.note: involving means surrounding, so the slander word goes around the other

parts.note: mud is slander, as in mud-slinging
a star is a big name, a celebrity

explanation.surface: Someone takes relish in slander involving a big-name celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relish' looks like a verb meaning enjoy; it is the noun, a condiment.
explanation.definitionFit: Mustard is a condiment, and a relish in the sense of a savoury sauce eaten with food.

clue.text: Wife turned up, about to fly off the handle

indicators.note: about means around, so the reversed title goes round to
in a down clue turned up means read upwards, so the title is reversed

parts.note: Mrs is the title of a married woman, a wife

explanation.surface: A wife turns up, ready to lose her temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned up' looks like 'arrived' in the surface; in a down clue it means read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To storm is to rage or show violent anger, an idiom-level match for losing one's temper.

clue.text: Joy, family member, runs away

indicators.note: away means gone, so the runs letter is taken out

parts.note: a relation is a family member
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Joy at a family member running away from home.
explanation.definitionFit: Elation is a feeling of great happiness and high spirits, a synonym of joy.

clue.text: Couple ultimately bound to run away together

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so the final letter of couple is taken

parts.note: its last letter is E
to lope is to bound along with long strides

explanation.surface: A couple who are ultimately bound to run away together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bound' looks like 'destined'; it means leap.
explanation.definitionFit: To elope is for lovers to flee secretly in order to marry.

clue.text: Taking issue over when work's done?

definitions.text: Taking issue over when work's done?

parts.words: Taking issue over when work's done?
parts.note: knocking can mean criticising or taking issue, so the phrase reads as complaining about the hour that ends a shift

explanation.walkthrough: Read as a whole, the clue suggests arguing about the end of the working day; split, 'knocking' means taking issue and the rest is the time work stops.
explanation.definitionFit: Knocking-off time is the informal British phrase for the hour when workers stop for the day.

clue.text: Distant meteor, rocky

indicators.note: rocky means unsteady, so the letters of meteor are shaken up

explanation.surface: A distant meteor, made of rock, is seen in the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rocky' looks like a description of the meteor, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Remote means far away, a direct synonym of distant.

clue.text: Member of the clergy looking embarrassed, having lost nerve inside

indicators.note: inside places the scrambled word within the colour word

parts.note: someone embarrassed looks red in the face

indicators.note: lost means astray, so the letters of nerve are rearranged

explanation.surface: A vicar goes red with embarrassment after losing his nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lost nerve' reads as losing courage, but 'lost' is the anagram signal on the word itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverend is a title and informal term for a minister or priest of the church.
